curatedList.text: First, on the nonprofit structure. A nonprofit is the primary governance decision. A for-profit Noesis would face exactly the incentive misalignment it is built to detect in others: the pressure to generate revenue from user data, engagement, and dependency rather than from mission. The structure is the demonstration. That said, we are not incorporated yet. We are pre-filing, and one of the concrete things we hope this challenge accelerates is access to the legal and institutional guidance that makes incorporation real. Second, on capacity and what we're actually asking for. I am a full-time Finance student at Texas Southern University and work full-time at a law firm. My co-founder Sanglee Baek is a working engineer in Seoul. We have built everything that exists, the introspection engine, the governance framework, the constitutional document, the KOSPI research platform, from within the margins. What I need from this challenge is the credibility and institutional momentum to establish a research lab at TSU dedicated to Noesis products, staffed by students who are learning what responsible AI governance looks like by building it. That lab is the scaling mechanism. Without it, Noesis grows only as fast as two people working in their spare time can carry it. Third, on why this matters now and not later. Governance frameworks for AI are ossifying. Infrastructure decisions made in the next 18 months, about agentic permissions, memory architecture, institutional accountability, will be extremely difficult to reverse once they are embedded in commercial products and regulatory expectations. The window to establish a constitutional standard for human-AI alignment that is architecturally enforced rather than policy-appended is real and it is narrowing. We are building Noesis because the alternative, AI systems that optimize around human values while appearing to serve them, is already the default, and the people positioned to govern that problem through law and policy need the technical infrastructure to point to. My long-run path is AI regulatory law and eventually the bench. Noesis is not a detour from that path. It is the foundation that makes that advocacy credible.

Yes. As we move into the next phase of the challenge, one important point to understand is that VIA’s value does not come from replacing smartphones, but from reducing friction in moments where smartphones are inconvenient. A common contradiction in the concept is that smartphones already give people constant access to digital tools. However, people still wear watches every day, even though phones can tell time. That behavior is not driven by necessity. It is driven by convenience, accessibility, and habit. Users adopt products that make repeated actions faster, easier, and less intrusive. VIA is built on that same principle. The goal is not to argue that people need another device, but that they will adopt one if it meaningfully reduces friction in daily interactions with AI, voice assistance, and real-time support. At this stage, we have already completed the initial MVP concept, core assumptions, and market research. However, funding is necessary to move from concept to execution and begin building the MVP. I have already prepared the cost estimates and supporting documents needed to outline what the MVP would require. While the hardware itself is not extremely costly, it still needs to be developed, tested, and packaged into a working prototype. Another important factor is marketing. A major part of VIA’s potential success depends not only on the technology, but on how the product is positioned. The concept must be communicated clearly as a convenience-driven, wearable AI interface that fits naturally into users’ daily lives. Strong branding, product storytelling, and go-to-market strategy will be essential to proving demand and helping users understand why VIA matters.

Our venture is anchored by a personal medical miracle that we believe elevates PetProof.ai beyond a comprehensive care assistant into a robust scientific discovery engine. A few years ago, Landry’s family and dogs were attacked by a massive swarm of aggressive hybrid bees. While she tragically lost one of their 100-lb dogs, the English Bulldog, Reno -- who had a recently diagnosed dime-sized malignant tumor on his eye waterline -- saw that tumor literally "fall off" and vanish within days of the attack, as if it had been surgically removed. It never returned. We have preserved the bee specimens and photographic evidence of this recovery. A key objective for this next phase is to use our institutional access to Texas A&M to facilitate a collaboration with the TAMU Entomology and Veterinary Medicine departments to examine these specimens. We want to investigate if this applied venom can be developed into a testable, injectable cancer solution for dogs. This mission to turn a freakishly bad tragedy into a lasting positive impact provides us with a proprietary research pipeline that generic agentic AI ventures cannot replicate, perfectly aligning with the Mays Business School vision of building a better future through business and AI. We are building PetProof.ai to ensure that the scientific miracle witnessed with Reno becomes a documented, testable reality for every pet owner, so that the next time a bizarre or high-stakes event unfolds, there is no more wondering who to call– because our platform will have already synthesized the research and verified the protocols needed to turn a crisis into a world-changing solution.

Three things worth knowing as Stage 1 begins: 1. Continuity through finals — I graduate from Virginia Tech in December 2026, which overlaps directly with the September 25-26 finals. Decision Intelligence has been my primary build for over a year, not a side project for this competition. 2. Pre-existing experiment culture — our local docs/EXPERIMENT_LOG.md already contains 69 entries in the same hypothesis / experiment / evidence / decision / impact format AIVVC's Learning Log uses. Stage 1 will accelerate this loop, not introduce it. 3. Warm-channel pilot transparency — our primary Stage 1 design-partner candidate is a Mexico-based EMS plant of a former employer (SPEEDTECH / Luxshare Precision) where I served as a HQ-to-site cross-site liaison. We are pursuing this warm channel in parallel with cold outreach to two US operations teams as plan B, and will disclose pilot scope honestly in our logs. We treat our SSRN working paper (DOI 10.2139/ssrn.6538460), production agent system, and prior experiment record as evidence, not as a closing argument, and welcome the external pressure Stage 1 will apply.

As a solo founder, I am approaching this challenge with a strong emphasis on disciplined experimentation and rapid learning. In the past two weeks, I have initiated clinical conversations with psychiatrists at Rutgers University Hospital, including a Chief Resident and the Vice-Chair of Clinical Affairs, to ground the venture in real clinical workflow and decision-making needs. These conversations have already shaped key aspects of the product, including prioritizing sleep and medication adherence signals and incorporating a pre-session behavioral alert into the summary. My focus for this phase is not just building, but systematically testing the highest-risk assumptions around signal reliability, clinician usability, and patient trust. I am intentionally starting with a narrow, clinically relevant scope to ensure that any prototype or insight generated is meaningful and actionable in a real psychiatric care setting.

A few things worth knowing as we move forward. I am a solo founder and a sophomore, which on paper looks like a liability. In practice it means every decision moves fast, there is no internal politics, and I have nothing pulling my attention away from making this work. The technical foundation for Vayumi is not theoretical. The voice pipeline, the memory layer, the intent classification, I have built and shipped real versions of all of these in production environments before this application existed. What I am building now is not starting from scratch. It is convergence. I also want to be honest about where I am. I do not have users yet. I do not have revenue. What I have is a clearly defined problem, a validated insight, a working architecture, and a level of conviction that has only grown the more I am ready for the next phase and I will make the most of whatever access and feedback this program offers.

AssignMate is not a class project or a pitch competition idea; it is a live, fully deployed platform that a real student built to solve a problem he was personally living. The GPA improvement and zero missed deadlines are not projected outcomes; they already happened. Every technical decision, from the AWS migration to the Supabase backend, was made under real constraints with real consequences. We are not here to learn whether we can build something. We already did. We are here to learn how to scale it, who will pay for it, and how to make it work for every student in Siouxland and beyond. We are coachable, we move fast, and we are committed to seeing this through all three stages. We would welcome any guidance, connections, or feedback the challenge can offer as we head into the summer.

Two things worth flagging as you evaluate Stage 1 progress: First, every metric in our submission is traceable. The 97.1% accuracy, 11,575-scenario test suite, 0% unsafe-failure rate, and 9/10 clinical safety rating are all from systems we built and logs we can show. We'd rather be questioned hard on methodology now than have a number unravel later. Second, we're aware of our sampling bias (52% of survey respondents under 25) and are correcting it in Wave 1 rather than waiting for a judge to find it. We'd rather flag known weaknesses than have them discovered. If there are specific assumptions or experiments the program wants us to prioritize or pressure-test, we'd welcome that direction, the experimentation roadmap is meant to be a starting point, not a fixed plan.

Watching a family friend sell his business in high school showed me what I wanted to do. So instead of traditional internships, I spent my entire college career inside lower middle market M&A, sitting across from real buyers and sellers, assessing deals, having countless conversations with searchers from programs like Booth, and working with top tech brokers. I even pursued my own acquisition of a 17-year-old home services business, which fell through in the transition period. Most recently I joined TWS Advisory, an M&A firm that has closed over a billion in transactions across the US, Middle East, and Africa, and in April I closed an SBA loan in 17 days, a record at a top national SBA lender. I'm still an undergrad. I'm not building Padre from a whiteboard.

Every enterprise AI company in our space is trying to convince regulated industries to trust their cloud. We're not asking for trust, we never touch their data in the first place. That's not a feature we built, it's an architectural decision we made on day one that our competitors cannot reverse without rebuilding everything. We're pre-revenue and pre-MVP right now. We know that. What we also know is that three law firm CTOs cited ABA Opinion 512 to us unprompted, Miami healthcare clinics told us federal law is the blocker , not budget and every single discovery conversation ended the same way: "when can we pilot this?" We're not the most polished team in this competition. We're the most problem-obsessed one. By June 30 you'll see the difference.

Is there anything else you would like us to know as we begin the next phase of the challenge? We are entering this next phase with a strong focus on learning through real users, not assumptions. Our goal is to continuously test, refine, and validate our core ideas using direct feedback and evidence from the field. We view AI as a core part of our venture-building process—not just for efficiency, but for improving the quality of our thinking, decisions, and iteration speed. We are especially focused on building a solution that is not only innovative, but also practical, scalable, and grounded in real community needs. Above all, we are committed to building with discipline, learning fast, and making measurable progress throughout the challenge.

Our primary objective for Stage 1 is to validate SecRecon’s technical and market viability by converting our initial private beta users into formal Letters of Intent (LOIs). Using an agentic Claude Code workflow to maintain high execution velocity, we will complete the development of our OAST-first autonomous verification module across AWS and Azure environments. By June, we aim to prove our core hypothesis: that providing "deterministic proof" of vulnerabilities reduces the security triage tax for MSPs by at least 80% compared to traditional probabilistic scanners. This evidence-based approach will allow us to transition from a technical prototype to a market-ready solution backed by documented customer demand.

I am committed to showing real progress through evidence-based experimentation, and I am grateful for the structure and accountability this challenge provides.

I am a solo founder, which means every decision, experiment, and learning cycle runs through me — but that also means I move fast, stay focused, and have full conviction in this mission. WealthIQ AI is not just a business idea for me — it is personal. I have seen firsthand how the lack of financial knowledge holds hardworking people back for generations. I am committed to using every resource this challenge offers — mentorship, feedback, and AI tools — to validate this venture as rigorously as possible and prove that closing the wealth gap through accessible financial intelligence is not just possible, but inevitable.

A quick note on how we operate, since it's a little unusual. CaseHug is a two-person team. Kevin Campbell, my tech advisor, builds the entire platform and we use AI as our process, which is why a two-person company has 114 API endpoints, 260+ document templates, and integrations with Clio and Smokeball already shipped. I own vision, sales, and go-to-market. We're a real test case for what a small team can build when AI is the development accelerator, not just a product feature. I figured that's worth flagging since the program is built around AI-as-accelerator.

Rooster is entering the next phase with a working prototype, strong founder-market fit, and early validation from the UMGC NEXUS Technology Track win, but we have reached the point where outside funding, mentorship, and structured experimentation are necessary to move from prototype to pilot-ready product.
